## Task 4 - Basic R Operations

### 1. Square root of 10
```{r}
sqrt(10)
```
The square root of 10 is 3.162.

### 2. Logarithm of 32 to base 2
```{r}
log(32, base = 2)
```
This returns 5, because 2^5 = 32.

### 3. Sum of numbers 1 to 1000
```{r}
sum(seq(1, 1000))
```
The sum of all integers from 1 to 1000 is 500,500.

### 4. Sum of even numbers from 2 to 1000
```{r}
sum(seq(2, 1000, 2))
```
By specifying a step of 2 starting from 2, seq() generates only even numbers.
The sum is 250,500.

### 5. Pairwise comparisons for 100 genes
```{r}
choose(100, 2)
```
Order does not matter for a pairwise comparison — gene A vs gene B is the
same as gene B vs gene A — so we use combinations. There are 4,950 possible
pairwise comparisons for 100 genes.

### 6. Ways to arrange 100 genes in triples
```{r}
factorial(100) / factorial(100 - 3)
```
Unlike pairwise comparisons, arrangements imply order matters — gene A→B→C
is distinct from gene C→B→A. This uses the permutations formula n!/(n-k)!.
There are 970,200 ways to arrange 100 genes in triples. 

## Task 5 - Using R Example Datasets

### 1-2. Loading and describing the CO2 dataset
```{r}
data("CO2")
head(CO2)
```
Data talks about CO2 uptake in grass plants. It has 84 rows and 5 columns
of data and is from an experiment on the cold tolerance of a grass species. 

### 3. Average and median CO2 uptake by region
```{r}
quebec <- CO2[CO2$Type == "Quebec", ]
mississippi <- CO2[CO2$Type == "Mississippi", ]

mean(quebec$uptake)
median(quebec$uptake)
mean(mississippi$uptake)
median(mississippi$uptake)
```
Quebec plants had a mean uptake of 33.54 and median of 37.15 umol/m^2/sec.
Mississippi plants had a mean uptake of 20.88 and median of 19.30 umol/m^2/sec.

## Task 6 - R Functions

### 1
```{r}
mean_median_ratio <- function(x) {
  result <- mean(x) / median(x)
  return(result)
}
```
Divides the mean by the median

### 2
```{r}
ignore_top_bottom_mean <- function(x) {
  x_trimmed <- x[x != min(x) & x != max(x)]
  result <- mean(x_trimmed)
  return(result)
}
```
Removes the max and min and gives the mean of the rest of the values 

### 3-4
Pipes (%>%) pass the output of one function directly into the next.
Use them for sequential data transformations. Avoid pipes when there are multiple 
inputs/outputs per step, or when steps are not linear

Apply functions (apply, lapply, sapply) replace loops by applying a 
function across rows, columns, or list elements simultaneously. They 
make code more concise and readable. Useful when running the same 
operation across multiple genes, samples, or datasets, which is common 
in genomics workflows.

## Task 7 - Basic Visualization with R

### 7.1a - Height distribution histograms

```{r}
library(remotes)
library(ggplot2)
magic_guys <- read.csv("magic_guys.csv")

# Base R histogram
jedi <- magic_guys[magic_guys$species == "jedi", ]
sith <- magic_guys[magic_guys$species == "sith", ]

hist(jedi$length, breaks=20, 
     main="Jedi height distribution", 
     xlab="Height")

hist(sith$length, breaks=20, 
     main="Sith height distribution", 
     xlab="Height")

# ggplot histogram
ggplot(magic_guys, aes(x=length, fill=species)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, alpha=0.6, position="dodge") +
  labs(title="Height distribution by species", 
       x="Height", 
       y="Count")
```

### 7.1b - Boxplots

```{r}
ggplot(magic_guys, aes(x=species, y=length, fill=species))+
    geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title="Height distribution by species (boxplots)", x="Species", y="Height")
```

### 7.1c - Saving plots

```{r}
# PNG - for web/presentations, small file size
png("height_boxplot.png")
ggplot(magic_guys, aes(x=species, y=length, fill=species))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title="Height distribution by species (boxplots)", x="Species", y="Height")
dev.off()

# PDF - for publications, infinitely scalable
pdf("height_boxplot.pdf")
ggplot(magic_guys, aes(x=species, y=length, fill=species))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title="Height distribution by species (boxplots)", x="Species", y="Height")
dev.off()

# SVG - for editing in Illustrator/Inkscape
svg("height_boxplot.svg")
ggplot(magic_guys, aes(x=species, y=length, fill=species))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title="Height distribution by species (boxplots)", x="Species", y="Height")
dev.off()
```
PNG is appropriate for digital use where file size matters. PDF is the 
standard for academic publications as it is vector-based and scales 
without pixelation. SVG is useful when the figure needs further editing 
in vector graphics software such as Inkscape or Adobe Illustrator.

### 7.2a - Microarray matrix dimensions

```{r}
microarray <- read.table("microarray_data.tab", header=TRUE, sep="\t")
dim(microarray)
head(microarray[, 1:5])
```

### 7.2b - Missing values per gene

```{r}
na_counts <- colSums(is.na(microarray))

ggplot(data.frame(gene=names(na_counts), na_count=na_counts),
       aes(x=na_count)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=50) +
  labs(title="Missing values per gene",
       x="Number of missing values",
       y="Number of genes")
```

### 7.2c - Genes exceeding missingness thresholds

```{r}
genes_10 <- names(na_counts[na_counts > 0.1 * nrow(microarray)])
genes_20 <- names(na_counts[na_counts > 0.2 * nrow(microarray)])
genes_50 <- names(na_counts[na_counts > 0.5 * nrow(microarray)])
```
### 7.2d - Imputing missing values with gene mean

```{r}
microarray_imputed <- as.data.frame(apply(microarray, 2, function(x) {
  x[is.na(x)] <- mean(x, na.rm=TRUE)
  return(x)
}))
```

### 7.3 - CO2 dataset visualisation

```{r}
ggplot(CO2, aes(x=conc, y=uptake, color=Type, linetype=Treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE) +
  labs(title="CO2 uptake vs concentration by type and treatment",
       x="CO2 concentration (mL/L)",
       y="CO2 uptake (umol/m^2/sec)")
```
Plotting uptake against concentration, split by both Type and Treatment,
reveals several patterns not visible from summary statistics alone. Uptake
increases with concentration but plateaus at higher levels, showing 
diminishing returns. Quebec plants consistently show higher uptake than 
Mississippi plants. Chilling reduces uptake more severely in 
Mississippi plants than Quebec plants suggesting that Quebec plants have greater cold tolerance. 

## Task 8 - Tidybiology Package

### Installation and loading
```{r}
library(tidybiology)
library(tidyverse)

data(chromosome)
data(proteins)

head(chromosome)
head(proteins)
```
The chromosome dataset contains 24 rows (one per chromosome) and 14 variables
including chromosome length, number of variations, protein coding genes, and 
various RNA types. The proteins dataset contains ~20,000 human proteins with 
variables including sequence, length, and mass.

### 8a - Summary statistics for chromosome data
```{r}
summary_statistic <- chromosome %>%
  summarise(
    mean_variations = mean(variations),
    median_variations = median(variations),
    max_variations = max(variations),
    mean_proteincoding = mean(protein_codinggenes),
    median_proteincoding = median(protein_codinggenes),
    max_proteincoding = max(protein_codinggenes),
    mean_mirna = mean(mi_rna),
    median_mirna = median(mi_rna),
    max_mirna = max(mi_rna)
  )
print(summary_statistic)
```

### 8b - Chromosome size distribution
```{r}
ggplot(chromosome, aes(x=basepairs)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=10, fill="steelblue") +
  labs(title="Chromosome size distribution",
       x="Base pairs",
       y="Count")
```

### 8c - Protein coding genes and miRNA vs chromosome length
```{r}
ggplot(chromosome, aes(x=basepairs, y=protein_codinggenes, label=id)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm") +
  geom_text(nudge_y=50) +
  labs(title="Protein coding genes vs chromosome length",
       x="Chromosome length (bp)",
       y="Number of protein coding genes")

ggplot(chromosome, aes(x=basepairs, y=mi_rna, label=id)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm") +
  geom_text(nudge_y=4) +
  labs(title="miRNA count vs chromosome length",
       x="Chromosome length (bp)",
       y="Number of miRNAs")
```
Both protein coding genes and miRNA counts show a positive correlation with 
chromosome length — larger chromosomes tend to contain more genes and miRNAs.

### 8d - Protein length vs mass
```{r}
summary_statistic_2 <- proteins %>%
  summarise(
    mean_length = mean(length),
    median_length = median(length),
    max_length = max(length),
    mean_mass = mean(mass),
    median_mass = median(mass),
    max_mass = max(mass)
  )
print(summary_statistic_2)

ggplot(proteins, aes(x=length, y=mass)) +
  geom_point(alpha=0.4, color="steelblue", size=1) +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", color="orchid3") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title="Protein mass vs length (log scale)",
       x="Protein length (amino acids, log scale)",
       y="Protein mass (Da, log scale)")
```
Protein mass and length show a near-perfect linear correlation on a log-log 
scale, consistent with the fact that protein mass is directly determined by 
amino acid composition and count. Log scaling was applied to both axes to reveal
the distribution of the bulk of proteins, which are compressed into the bottom
left of untransformed plot.
